## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāpanādajātaka* (Ja 264) is a canonical Jātaka tale of the Pali Tipiṭaka [SuttaCentral]. The verses open with the incipit *Panādo nāma so rājā* (“’Twas king Panāda”) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework recorded in the text and its commentary, the Buddha related this story while seated on the bank of the Ganges, occasioning his teaching by the miraculous psychic power (*ānubhāva*) of the Elder Bhaddaji [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The introductory account traces this event to the Master traveling from Sāvatthī to Bhaddiyanagara and residing in the Jātiyāvana to assist Bhaddaji [Fausböll 1879]. Within the broader Jātaka narrative cycle, King Mahāpanāda is recognized as the son of Suruci and a king reigning at Mithilā in the realm of Videha [Fausböll 1897].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral link the verses of Ja 264 directly to the *Theragāthā*, specifically the verses of Elder Bhaddaji (Thag 2.22, *Bhaddajittheragāthā*) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects internal Pali text reuse across several commentarial corpora, matching segments of Ja 264 (§0.4–3.4) with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, the Dīghanikāya *Pāthikavagga-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. The alignment with the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* corroborates the canonical parallel identified by SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus reports no cross-language parallels meeting the threshold of score 10 or higher [DharmaNexus].
